teaching.causalExplanation: The Earth spins once a day. That's a full turn, three hundred and sixty degrees, in twenty-four hours. Divide, and every hour it turns fifteen degrees. So fifteen degrees of longitude is one hour of time. Watch the noon line sweep. Every hour, it moves another fifteen degrees west. We can go smaller, too. One hour is sixty minutes, and sixty divided by fifteen is four, so one degree of longitude is four minutes of time. Move one degree east, and the Sun's noon comes four minutes sooner. Fifteen degrees is an hour, and one degree is four minutes. And because the Earth spins towards the east, the Sun always reaches the eastern place first. So the place further east is ahead, and the place further west is behind. Let's use it. Sydney is at about a hundred and fifty-one degrees east, and Perth at about a hundred and sixteen degrees east. Both are east of Greenwich, on the same side, so subtract to find the gap. A hundred and fifty-one minus a hundred and sixteen is thirty-five degrees. Each degree is four minutes, so thirty-five degrees is a hundred and forty minutes, two hours and twenty minutes. Or divide by fifteen, and you get two and a third hours, the same thing. Careful, two and a third hours is two hours twenty, not two hours thirty-three, because a third of sixty minutes is twenty. Sydney is further east, so it's ahead. When the Sun says noon in Sydney, it says nine forty in Perth. Now here's the surprise. Real clocks in Perth are two hours behind Sydney on standard time, three during daylight saving, and never two hours twenty. Regions round their clocks to whole hours, or sometimes half hours, so everyone in a region shares one time. Longitude gives the Sun's time. The clocks are a choice, and that's coming up. The same idea explains a number you'll see a lot. The meridian at a hundred and fifty degrees east is a hundred and fifty degrees from Greenwich. A hundred and fifty divided by fifteen is ten, so it's ten hours ahead of Greenwich. When it's noon at Greenwich, it's ten pm there. A place at a hundred and five degrees east is seven hours ahead, so noon at Greenwich is seven pm there. And Sydney, at a hundred and fifty-one east, is one degree past a hundred and fifty, so by the Sun it's ten hours and four minutes ahead of Greenwich. That's why the clocks in eastern Australia are set ten hours ahead of Greenwich, the nearest whole hour, before any daylight saving.

scenes.teachingReason: What if the two places are on opposite sides of Greenwich, one east and one west? Then the gap runs through nought, so you add. Tokyo is at about a hundred and forty degrees east, and New York at about seventy-four degrees west. A hundred and forty plus seventy-four is two hundred and fourteen degrees. Times four minutes, that's eight hundred and fifty-six minutes, which is fourteen hours sixteen minutes. Tokyo is east, so it's ahead. If it's nine am on Wednesday in Tokyo, take off fourteen hours sixteen. Going back past midnight takes you into the day before. So by longitude, it's six forty-four pm on Tuesday in New York. When a time difference crosses midnight, check the day as well as the time.

scenes.teachingReason: Two slips catch people here. The first is subtracting when the places are on opposite sides. Seventy-four from a hundred and forty is sixty-six degrees, which would put New York only four hours twenty-four behind Tokyo, and that's far too close. The second is the direction. Adding the hours to the western place puts it ahead, but the Sun reaches the east first, so east is always ahead.

scenes.teachingReason: So that's longitude and time. Fifteen degrees an hour, and east ahead. But remember the surprise. Real clocks don't follow every degree. Australia shares just three time zones, each with one time on its clocks, rounded from the Sun's time, and some states move their clocks in summer while others don't. How do Australian time zones and daylight saving work? That's next.
